newsitem.title: USA: Chinese activists at low point, dissident says.
newsitem.headline: Chinese activists at low point, dissident says.

text.p: Chinese dissident Wang Xizhe, who recently fled to the United States, said on Tuesday that China's pro-democracy movement was at a "low point" because of worsening repression by the authorities.
In an interview with Reuters, Wang also said that he still wanted to join Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang, even though most of his friends opposed the idea.
"I feel that the political repression (in China) has been getting more serious every day. Any expression of opinion has been prosecuted," Wang said through an interpreter.

He singled out former student leader Wang Dan, who has been accused of plotting to overthrow the government, and of pro-democracy activist Liu Xiaobo, who was recently arrested and sentenced to three years in a labor camp.

One of China's leading dissidents, Wang fled his home in China's Guangdong province this month, days after Liu's arrest. Wang and Liu had recently written a letter criticizing the Chinese government. Wang, 46, went first to Hong Kong and flew to the San Francisco area last week.

"Because of oppression by the Chinese government, all the dissidents that I know of are facing extreme difficulties and I believe it is a low point in the democratic movement," Wang said. He said there was also a lack of cohesion among the democracy movement's supporters overseas and he hoped to do something to improve that situation.
Wang appealed to "the whole world" to maintain its interest in Liu and Wang Dan and said he hoped the American government would continue to use its "good offices" in their cases.

Wang said, however, that while the pro-democracy movement was very thankful for the support given it by the U.S. and European governments, "we feel that we are not in a position to make any further demands on them ... As to the future, we feel that we have to depend on our own work."
Wang said most of his friends opposed his plan, announced on Monday, to apply to join the Kuomintang (KMT).

"My friends are of the opinion that the KMT is totally an organization of the past ... I have thought this matter over for a long time and I will not change my opinion now," he said. However, he said he would take a few days to explain to his friends what he hoped to achieve by joining the KMT.
Taiwan's Nationalist Party said earlier Tuesday that it would welcome Wang into the party if he voiced support for Taiwan's Republic of China government.
Wang said he understood that Taiwan officials had asked him to recognize the Chinese nationalist government on Taiwan as valid and he said he was prepared to do that.

Wang said he wanted to join the KMT precisely because it was unusual for a Chinese dissident to do so. "There has been a stalemate between the Taiwan and mainland movements and the gap is very big and I believe by joining the KMT, I can form a communication channel between the two," he said.
He said he wanted to go to study the situation in Taiwan "but at this point I still believe that I would like to live in the U.S.," he said.
Wang said he planned to travel to New York in a few days and then to Washington D.C. to meet with members of the democracy movement and their supporters.

Wang's activism dates from 1974 when he co-authored an attack in Guangdong on the radical 1966-76 Cultural Revolution. He took part in the 1979 Democracy Wall movement in Beijing and produced his own dissident newsletters. He was twice imprisoned and spent 17 years in jail and labor camps. He was released on parole in 1993.
